The answer is O. Hemolytic disease of the newborn is a condition that can affect a fetus of an rhesus or ABO incompatibile mother. The mother's immune system can create IgG antibodies against the rhesus antigens or ABO antigens that are present in the fetus' blood. These antibodies can cross the placenta and enter the fetus' bloodstream. If the antibodies are against the rhesus antigens, the mother must be rhesus negative and the fetus must be rhesus positive. This can happen if the mother has been sensitised, i.e. has had previous pregnancy, miscarriage or transfusion with rhesus positive blood. If the antibodies are against the ABO antigens, the mother must be blood type O, A or B and the fetus must be blood type AB. The mother's immune system creates IgG antibodies against the ABO antigens if exposed to them in the pregnancy. The antibodies cross the placenta and enter the fetus' bloodstream. The fetus' immune system then mounts an immune response to the foreign antibodies and antigens, causing haemolysis of the fetus' own RBCs. This leads to anaemia in the fetus, which can be fatal. The anaemia causes the body to release fluid into the tissues in an attempt to compensate, which leads to oedema. The increased haemolysis also causes jaundice due to increased bilirubin levels.

In the small intestine, Cl- is pumped out of enterocytes by the NBC (Na+/HCO3- pump) and this causes water to follow by osmosis. This creates a positive lumen potential and a negative serosal potential, which drives the diffusion of Na+ into the enterocytes via ENaC (epithelial sodium channels). The Na+ then binds to the Na+/K+ ATPase which pumps 3Na+ in for every K+ out. This creates a low Na+ concentration in the lumen and a high concentration in the enterocytes. This is important as it allows Na+ to be reabsorbed from the lumen into the blood.  In the pancreas, the process is similar up until the Na+/K+ ATPase. Here, the pump is not able to pump Na+ back into the blood and so the Na+ concentration in the lumen is low. This is important as it allows HCO3- to be secreted into the ducts. Low Na+ concentration means that water cannot follow by osmosis into the lumen and so HCO3- can be secreted without losing too much water.  In cystic fibrosis, the CFTR is dysfunctional and so Cl- cannot diffuse out of the enterocytes. This means that water is not drawn out of the enterocytes by osmosis and so Na+ is not reabsorbed. This means that Na+ concentration in the lumen is high and so water follows by osmosis into the lumen. This means that HCO3- cannot be secreted into the ducts and so the pancreas is vulnerable to infection.
